climbing_route.label: Traverse to the south col (~7,480 ft)
climbing_route.notes: The classic guidebook line gains the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak and traverses onto Agnes' south ridge. From an Icy-Spruce Pass high camp the travelled variation goes over Point 7458, drops to a notch near 7,200 ft, crosses a snowfield at the head of Yew Creek, then climbs a steep, narrow snow couloir on the south side of Agnes for roughly 1,300 ft to the south col at about 7,480 ft. Carry axe and crampons: this couloir has been found firm and steep, and it is the descent line as well. Late in the season expect a moat where the snow pulls away from the rock at the top.

climbing_route.label: Lower south ridge
climbing_route.notes: Rope up. Several short pitches on or just left of the ridge crest, on rock that is broken and demands testing. Where the crest steepens past reason, the usual solution is to lose about a pitch to a ledge system on the west side and traverse north beneath the difficulties to a rubbly whaleback — the first place the summit block comes into view. Route-finding here is the real difficulty; committing to the crest can leave a party downclimbing loose ground under load.

climbing_route.label: Summit block ramp
climbing_route.notes: From the col the way onto the summit block is a broad ramp immediately left of a distinctive snow-filled gully. Follow it up and dog-leg right toward the headwall. Do not try to stay on the crest above: it is blocked by a large horn. Rockfall generated by a party above is the main hazard on the ramp.

climbing_route.label: Crux chimney
climbing_route.notes: Two chimneys break the headwall out of the snow gully. The left-hand, more obvious one has been found impassable; the second, immediately right, is the one that goes and is the hardest climbing on the peak. Its grade is reported anywhere from 5.6 to 5.8 depending on party and conditions — treat 5.8 as the planning figure. Rock quality is poor: holds have been reported moving under hand, so test everything and belay from out of the fall line. Snow or ice in the back of the chimney early in the season adds significantly to the difficulty.

climbing_route.label: Upper wall and summit
climbing_route.notes: One further roped pitch above the chimney, then roughly 100 ft of exposed scrambling on the west side of the block to the top. Loose rock and real exposure — most parties stay roped. Descent is by two or three rappels back down the summit block, then the south couloir on running belays for about 1,400 ft; the moat at the top of that couloir and the loose ground beside it are where parties knock rock onto each other, so descend one at a time or well spaced. Agnes is climbed only every few years, so anchors and any fixed gear should be treated as unknown and replaced.

climbing_route.label: Snow and glacier margin below the Buckner-Booker col
climbing_route.notes: The northwest route is gained from the col between Buckner and Booker. The upper snow and the glacier margin below the col hold crevasses — parties have bypassed open cracks on snow bridges here, and one such bridge collapsed on a party within a week of another crossing it, with climbers on both sides. Rope up for this section, sound the bridges, and consider going early while the snow is frozen. Some parties reach the same ground from the Horseshoe Basin side, traversing rock slabs that run with meltwater and are slick.

climbing_route.label: Gully below the col, west of the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the col, a north-facing gully leads toward the summit with one short class 3 step. The gully holds loose blocks; keep to one side rather than the gut, and avoid stacking a party directly above another — rockfall released by climbers above is the principal hazard on the route. Snow can linger in the gully well into summer.

climbing_route.label: Talus and scree to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Cut right out of the gully onto low-angle talus and scree slopes and walk these to the summit; the route as a whole is class 2/3 with no technical rock. The route-finding trap is leaving the gully too early and ending above a short wall on the west, which forces an awkward traverse on small ledges back into the line. Descent reverses the route — the col and its snow bridges are the crux both ways, and Booker sees roughly one party a year, so expect no boot track and no cairns.

wa_cathedral_rock_northwest_couloir.skip_reason: The only published beta found for this specific line is a single sentence naming the NW Couloir as probably the easiest route on the peak and citing the guidebook grade as class 3. Nothing found describes the couloir's length, the exit onto the summit block, the rock, the snow conditions or the descent. Everything else available online describes the Southwest Face route instead. Writing a segment list from that one sentence would mean inventing the climbing, so the section is left empty.

climbing_route.label: Notch to the west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the low notch on the Cinderella-Little Sister ridge, step off the Green Creek (Sisters) Glacier and onto rock. This is where parties stow glacier gear. Watch the moat at the glacier margin: it is trivial in a heavy snow year and a real obstacle late in the season, and it is the same problem in reverse on the way down. Do not be tempted along the crest toward Little Sister — that continuation has been judged loose and hazardous and is normally avoided.

climbing_route.label: West ridge to the true summit
climbing_route.notes: The long west ridge is mostly straightforward walking on broken ground with a short section of enjoyable scrambling to reach the true summit. Taking the crest absolutely direct runs into stretches of committing downclimbing; the standard escape is to drop into a gully on the south side and regain easier terrain above. The rock here is dunite, unusual in the Cascades — it is notably grippy on weathered surfaces but greasy where a block has freshly broken, so judge each hold on its surface rather than on the rock type.

climbing_route.label: Descent to the glacier
climbing_route.notes: Two descents are in use off the north side. Parties have downclimbed clean slabs directly to the edge of the glacier — steeper-looking from above than it climbs, with a passage at each apparent crux — and parties have also rappelled the north face, which has gone with a single double-rope rappel landing on a steep snow panel above the glacier. Carry two ropes if the rappel is the plan. On the snow panel below, an axe and crampons are wanted; the moat at its base is the last obstacle.

climbing_route.label: Saddle to the upper east face
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle west of the peak the line goes onto the upper east face and east ridge. Cairns mark the way where the terrain is ambiguous, and the traverse into the face crosses loose ground before it improves. No technical rock and no serious glacier travel is required on this peak, but the terrain is rough throughout — talus, sidehill traversing and occasional lingering snowfields, and a small snow patch or the Kimtah Glacier margin may have to be crossed depending on season and which saddle is used.

climbing_route.label: Upper east face to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A couple of hundred feet of third-class scrambling on rock that is reported mostly solid finishes at the summit. Descent normally reverses the line; parties continuing to a col on the far side have plunge-stepped scree and then downclimbed a talus-choked gully, described as steep and tedious enough that it is better as a descent than an ascent. Cosho is remote and rarely visited, so route-finding in poor visibility is the main hazard — carry the ability to navigate back to the correct gully, since the wrong one leads into brush.

climbing_route.label: Dark Fin Col onto the glacier
climbing_route.notes: At the col, harness up and put on glacier gear before moving. Gaining the Dark Glacier means descending a loose slope off the col — poor footing over the glacier, and the place where a party strung out above another will send rock down. This is also the crux on the return, tired and often in the afternoon.

climbing_route.label: Dark Glacier, roughly 7,000 to 8,250 ft
climbing_route.notes: The glacier is genuinely crevassed and roped travel with crevasse rescue capability is the expectation; it runs from about 8,200 down to 6,800 ft. Route-finding matters as much as the crevasses: the line has to be picked to stay out from under wet-loose runouts coming off snow slabs perched on wet rock along the margins, so avoid the temptation to hug the rock for easier walking.

climbing_route.label: Moat crossing onto the rock ridge
climbing_route.notes: Leave the glacier around 8,250 ft by crossing the moat onto the rock of the summit ridge. This crossing is normally belayed — the gap and the quality of its lip vary through the season, and it can be the single hardest move of the climb late in a dry year.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: By roughly late June the final ridge traverse is bare rock and the finish is a straightforward walk up scree to the summit. Early in the season the same traverse can be heavily snow-covered and is reported as dicey, with cornices to be expected along the crest — stay well back from the edge and treat an early-season attempt as a different, more serious proposition. Descent reverses the route, with the moat and the loose slope back up to the col the two places to allow time for.

climbing_route.label: Lower buttress start
climbing_route.notes: The direct start takes the buttress head-on rather than escaping into the glacier couloir on the left, and that is the reason to be here: the couloir alternative is loose and largely unprotectable, with rockfall a repeated problem, while the buttress rock is clean and takes gear. Two slabby pitches on cracks around 5.8 lead to the crux roof at 5.10-. Grade V overall, about 2,200 ft and 21 pitches — this is a full day of climbing on top of a multi-day approach, so start early and know your bail options, which are poor.

climbing_route.label: Chimneys and rightward traverses
climbing_route.notes: Chimney systems above the roof lead into a series of traverses. The traversing pitches hold loose blocks and are the section most often called out as unpleasant: a block pulled here goes onto the belayer and onto anyone below, and traversing ground is also where a fall is worst for the follower. Extend runners, protect the second, and take care over what you weight.

climbing_route.label: Mid-buttress face climbing
climbing_route.notes: Face climbing and a left-hand crack system carry the route up the middle of the wall. This is where the rock can be wet from snowmelt draining the upper mountain — the same holds that are positive dry become slick, and the slabbier sequences are the ones that suffer. A cool, dry spell before the trip matters more here than on most Cascade rock.

climbing_route.label: Offwidth on the crest
climbing_route.notes: The buttress crest gives the second crux, an offwidth that is awkward with a pack on and has some fixed gear in it. A variation starts up the offwidth and then traverses right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8, belaying back at the top of the wide section — worth knowing about if the leader is climbing with a haul-free pack. A large cam (to about a 4) is the piece that makes the direct version comfortable.

climbing_route.label: Upper buttress to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Above the offwidth the crest continues at 5.9, then a long pitch of thin cracks around 5.10- to a small stance, and the remaining pitches ease off along the buttress to the ridgeline. From there most parties unrope and move together up fourth and easy fifth class ground, trending right, to gain the ridge that runs left to the summit. Rack: a full set of cams to a 4 with doubles in the mid sizes and plenty of slings; a single rope is enough because the descent is a walk-off. Descent goes west on third and fourth class terrain, roughly an hour, then down a short third-class gully to the north and through snow slopes and cliff bands back to camp — do this in daylight if at all possible, as the cliff bands are the part that goes wrong in the dark.

climbing_route.label: Lower Chimney Glacier to the upper glacier
climbing_route.notes: Rope up at the toe and climb the lower glacier. Three ways have been used to break through the cliff band onto the upper glacier; the common one is the rock and snow gully just left of the icefall. Crevasses and the icefall are the hazards, and the gully can be running with meltwater later in the day — an early start pays here twice over.

climbing_route.label: Upper glacier and the moat
climbing_route.notes: Cross the upper glacier to the east face directly beneath the summit. A moat routinely forms where the ice pulls away from the rock and it is the crux of getting on the route: in some conditions collapsed ice blocks have bridged it into a usable ramp and platform, in others it needs a belayed step across or a detour. Assess this from a distance on the way in, because the alternative is a long traverse looking for a way on.

climbing_route.label: Ledge systems to the Key Ledge
climbing_route.notes: One pitch from the glacier gains a broad heather ledge system. From its right side, a leftward-sloping ledge system links faces and gullies toward the north end of the prominent Key Ledge two thirds up the face. Most of this is exposed third-class walking on ledges with a few short fourth-class steps, often on wet rock, and running belays are the usual compromise between speed and safety. Reckon on about four hours from the glacier. The Key Ledge itself is a bivy for around six people, though water on it is unreliable.

climbing_route.label: Summit pitches
climbing_route.notes: Three pitches of class 4 and low fifth class slabs finish the climb, roughly two and a half hours from the ledge, with the hardest moves around 5.4 to 5.6 — Grade II overall. The first pitch takes low-fifth ground on generally sound rock and protects adequately with slings, stoppers and small cams up to about three quarters of an inch. Above it a short traverse crosses a small heathered ledge onto a very exposed fourth-class face. The last pitch is a clean low-fifth chimney that tops out a few feet from the summit cairn. Rock shoes are worth carrying for this section.

climbing_route.label: Rappel descent
climbing_route.notes: Descent is by rappel down the line of ascent: two rappels from the summit back to the Key Ledge, then on the order of six more to reach the glacier, with anchors reported in place and serviceable the whole way. A single 165 ft rope has been sufficient. Back the anchors up rather than trusting old tat, keep the ropes clear of the loose ledges, and leave enough daylight — the moat crossing back onto the glacier is the last problem of the day, not the first.
